title: DataBook
description: Why I built DataBook and a worked example using Pokémon base stats.

conventions.population: 721 Pokémon, one per National Dex number, from Generations I–VI.
notes: Keep the first source row for each National Dex number.

rows.body:
## Why I made it

I wanted a way to share a data analysis that people could explore for themselves. In DataBook, I can write up a finding, put an interactive chart beside it, and give readers a way to trace the chart back to its data.

## How it works

A DataBook organizes Markdown and charts into pages and tabs. Each chart declares a query against one shared table. DataBook runs the query in the browser and passes the result to a React chart. The repo includes a starter and a skill that guides coding agents through building and extending a book.

Open **Sample DataBook** to compare Pokémon, explore stat distributions, and see how the charts are built from one dataset.

[View DataBook on GitHub](https://github.com/kdopenshaw/databook)

## Similar totals can hide very different strengths

Alakazam and Shuckle both total about 500. Alakazam puts 135 points into Special Attack and 120 into Speed. Shuckle has 230 in each defense and just 5 in Speed. Pick two Pokémon to see where their points go.

## Speed is only one way to spend a stat budget

Each point represents a Pokémon. Filter by primary type to see how much Speed varies among Pokémon with similar totals.

## Legendary Pokémon have higher totals, with some overlap

The median base stat total is **600** for the 46 Pokémon flagged as legendary and **410** for the other 675. The groups overlap from 580 to 670 points.

## Electric averages 83.5 Speed across 36 species

Flying ranks first at **96.3**, based on just three primary-Flying Pokémon. Electric leads among types with at least ten species. Fairy averages **48.6** across 17.

rows.body:
## From Pokédex to chart

[Pokémon with stats](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/abcsds/pokemon) contains 800 rows for 721 National Dex numbers across Generations I–VI. This analysis keeps the first row for each number to avoid counting alternate forms as extra species. Legendary status comes from the dataset. Base stats are game parameters and do not measure battle outcomes.

All four charts use a single [canonical table](https://github.com/kdopenshaw/databook/blob/main/src/data/canonical.json). In [the book definition](https://github.com/kdopenshaw/databook/blob/main/src/data/rows.json), the distribution query bins stat totals and counts each group per bin. The Speed query groups by primary type and returns the mean Speed and species count. The radar query selects twelve species. The scatter plot shows all species and lets you filter by primary type. DataBook passes those results to React chart components.
